diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $E$ be a convex, compact subset of $[0,+\infty)\times[0,+\infty)$.
The discretisations and parameters used for the ADMM are exactly the same of Section \ref{sec:test_dal}, as well as the interaction kernel.

issues.failure_explanation: The operative kernel is negative for 0≤r<1/4, so sufficiently similar agents repel. For example, take N=2, E={(0,0)}, and initial colours (0,1). Then r12=0, φ(0)=−1, and the initial derivatives are (−1/2,1/2), immediately leaving the grey-level interval [0,1]. The profile also initially increases with distance rather than decreasing. This is a failure of the stated evolution, not merely an incorrect kernel name.

failure_location.quote: In particular, each agent tends to align its state $c_i$ with the states of nearby agents whose intensities are similar, while the strength of this influence decays with spatial distance.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require a nonnegative, distance-decreasing interaction profile and replace the operative kernel accordingly, for example by (1+4r)(1−r)^4 on nonnegative arguments up to the cutoff, with a compatible extension. Verify or recompute the trajectories and optimizations using the repaired kernel.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised alignment, preservation of valid grey levels, and interpretation of simulations using this kernel are unreliable.
issues.title: The specified kernel produces repulsion rather than the advertised alignment
issues.why_classification: A contained kernel replacement preserves the intended model architecture, but changes the actual dynamics and requires verification or recomputation of the numerical results.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\alpha > 0$. Then the functional $J : H^1(\Omega) \to \R$ in Definition \ref{def:cost_functional} has a unique global minimum.

issues.failure_explanation: The only existence theorem minimizes J over all H1 images, whereas the advertised problem minimizes over dynamically reachable terminal images. The unconstrained minimizer need not be reachable, even when E is a singleton. Compactness of the pointwise control set does not by itself prove attainment for measurable controls with nonlinear control dependence. No argument establishes the required closedness of the reachable set or existence of an ordinary optimal control.

failure_location.quote: We define a cost functional based on the $L^2$ norm of the intensity gradient, establish the well-posedness of the problem, and derive the corresponding optimality system.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the well-posedness conclusion to unconstrained minimization of J. Retaining the advertised optimal-control conclusion requires a separate existence theorem for the state/control formulation and its reachable terminal states.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed well-posedness of the continuous optimal-control problem is not established; Theorem thm:existence1 itself remains valid.
issues.title: Unconstrained image minimization does not establish optimal-control well-posedness
issues.why_classification: The source-supported weakening abandons the advertised optimal-control existence result; retaining it requires a separate control-existence argument rather than a local repair of the functional-minimization proof.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $E$ be a convex, compact subset of $[0,+\infty)\times[0,+\infty)$.
Here $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable interaction kernel that weighs the influence of neighbouring agents

issues.failure_explanation: Admissible controls may have either scale equal to zero, making the displayed reciprocal semi-axis undefined and the underlying quadratic sublevel set a cylinder or slab rather than a bounded ellipsoid. Compact support alone also need not be a full interval beginning at zero: an annular support produces an ellipsoidal shell. Intersecting these sets with the image domain does not restore the asserted ellipsoid.

failure_location.quote: When $\phi$ has compact support, the interaction domain is a bounded ellipsoid in $[0,1]^3$, centred at $p_i$ and with semi–axes proportional to $(\varepsilon_x(t)^{-1/2}, \varepsilon_x(t)^{-1/2}, \varepsilon_c(t)^{-1/2})$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Describe the interaction set directly through φ(r) and its intersection with the image domain. State the ellipsoid description only for positive scales and full interval support, and explicitly cover zero-scale and other support geometries.
issues.overall_effect: The geometric description does not cover the declared control and kernel classes.
issues.title: Compact support does not give the asserted nondegenerate ellipsoidal interaction domain
issues.why_classification: A local qualification of the geometric description preserves the model, admissible controls, and numerical procedures.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Moreover, $T$ should be large enough to enable the formation of clusters -- or, in the language of opinion dynamics, to let the agents reach consensus.

issues.failure_explanation: Even with a smooth compactly supported nonnegative kernel having φ(0)=1, the admissible control ε≡(0,0) gives, for two agents, d'(t)=−d(t), where d=c2−c1. Thus d(t)=d(0)e^(−t) never vanishes at finite time when d(0)≠0. Increasing a finite T cannot turn this asymptotic consensus into exact finite-time clustering.

failure_location.quote: Classical results for opinion dynamics models~\cite{MotschTadmor2014} ensure that, under mild assumptions on $\phi$, the solution converges to a finite number of clusters in finite time.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the finite-time assertion by an appropriately qualified asymptotic or tolerance-based statement and interpret finite-T outputs accordingly. Exact finite-time clusters would require an additional merging construction or different dynamics.
issues.overall_effect: Exact finite-time quantization and the recommendation to obtain exact consensus merely by choosing T sufficiently large are unsupported.
issues.title: Smooth consensus dynamics do not generally form exact clusters in finite time
issues.why_classification: The available correction changes the finite-time exact-output guarantee to an asymptotic or approximate one; the source provides no construction preserving the original guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For our purposes, we add a projection $\Pi_E$ onto the convex set $E$ to bound the control at each step.
However, when the control is constrained, the equality is not verified on the boundary of the compact set $E$.

issues.failure_explanation: At a lower active bound with positive gradient, projection can leave the control unchanged while the right-hand side demands a strict decrease proportional to the full gradient norm. No positive step can then pass. Active gradient components can also make this bound impossible away from constrained stationarity: for f(x,y)=Mx+y at (0,1/2) in [0,1]^2, the decrease is at most τ, whereas the required decrease is cτ(M²+1).

failure_location.quote: \WHILE{ $J(\Pi_E(\varepsilon^{(j)} - \tau^{(k)}\, D^{(j)} ) ) > J(\varepsilon^{(j)}) - c \,\tau^{(k)} |D^{(j)}|^2$ }

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a projection-aware sufficient-decrease condition based on the actual displacement, such as the gradient paired with ΠE(ε−τD)−ε, together with a projected-stationarity check.
issues.overall_effect: The shrinking line-search loop need not terminate for legitimate constrained iterates, independently of the final update sign.
issues.title: The projected Armijo test can reject every positive step
issues.why_classification: This is a standard local correction of projected backtracking and preserves the objective, control set, and intended descent method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: There exists a saddle point for the functional $L : H^1(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \to \R$ defined in \eqref{eq:cost_tv_regular}.
For analytical convenience, we assume that the image is continuous in both space and intensity

issues.failure_explanation: Take bounded smooth approximations u_n of a jump and v_n=∇u_n. Then L equals TV(u_n)+(α/2)||u_n−I||² and stays bounded, while ||u_n||H1 and ||v_n||2 diverge. Thus the claimed coercivity is false. H1 attainment can genuinely fail for continuous data: choose a continuous increasing one-dimensional u, flat near the boundary, with an interior non-H1 cusp, and a smooth p∈[0,1] equal to 1 where u increases and 0 at the boundary. For I=u−p'/α, with α sufficiently large and u bounded away from 0 and 1, I is admissible continuous data and p calibrates u as the unique TV minimizer. Smooth approximations reach its infimum, but no H1 function attains it. Extending these functions in the second coordinate gives the stated square domain.

failure_location.quote: Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:existence1}, it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, replace the false coercivity argument by a valid attainment theory with additional data regularity, or reformulate the TV problem in BV with appropriate gradient and dual spaces. Adding genuine H1 regularization would instead change the objective.
issues.overall_effect: Saddle-point existence, primal attainment, and the asserted attained strong-duality identity are not valid in the stated general H1/L2 setting.
issues.title: The saddle-point theorem lacks coercivity and can fail in the stated H1 space
issues.why_classification: The missing norm control is genuinely absent and admissible continuous data can yield nonattainment. Repair requires a changed analytic regime or functional-space architecture, not a corrected estimate.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In general, the saddle point is not unique.

issues.failure_explanation: All L2 multipliers are already feasible as variables, but that does not make them optimal dual variables or prove saddle nonuniqueness. For constant I, take u*=I, v*=0 and μ=2e1. The saddle value at this primal pair is zero, but choosing v=−se1 with 0<s<2/ρ gives L=−s+ρs²/2<0. Hence this μ does not make the primal pair minimizing. Saddle multipliers must also satisfy the primal subgradient and stationarity conditions.

failure_location.quote: In fact, when approaching the minimum point $(u^*,v^*)$ in the primal variables (which is unique), the term $\int_\Omega \mu \cdot (v^*-\nabla u^*)$ vanishes, so that any $\mu \in L^2(\Omega; \R^2)$ becomes feasible.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the feasibility argument by the KKT restrictions, including −μ∈∂|v| at feasibility and the u-stationarity condition, and describe only the nonuniqueness remaining within that restricted set.

issues.failure_explanation: Fix a constant image, so the state cannot change and ∇c=0. On a region where μ=me1 and |m|>1, shrinkage gives v=−(m−sign(m))e1/ρ. diagnostic_evidence.quote: This is the reason why Theorem \ref{thm:saddle_point} is fundamental: it ensures that there is no duality gap.

issues.failure_explanation: The difference between consecutive decreases and increases of an augmented Lagrangian is not a primal-dual gap and can vanish while feasibility fails. For the scalar split form L=|v|+μ(v−u)+(v−u)²/2+(u−a)²/2, 0<a<1, initialize (u,v,μ)=(a,0,0). One exact ADMM step with ρ=γ=1 gives (a/2,0,−a/2). The primal decrease and dual increase are both a²/4, but the constraint residual is −a/2. Thus this stopping logic fails even in the convex, exact-subsolve case, independently of the nonconvex duality issue.
